[36:34] Now for the modern contrast, building the Kentucky Ark required chainsaws, industrial sawmills, computerg guided cutting, trucks, 110 ton cranes, and dozens of full-time Amish carpenters. Even so, construction took nearly a year and a half and cost about $100 million. In the Netherlands, Johan Hibers spent years building his own full-scale ark in Dorrect, which opened in 2012. And to keep it afloat, he had to build it on top of a row of steel barges. Both are still there today. You can board the Kentucky Ark and walk across its three wooden decks.

[37:10] And Hibis' ark remains morowed in the water, floating on steel. There is one question no skeptic will overlook. Fine, the hull floats. But how could anyone survive inside? Thousands of animals confined in a wooden box for more than a year. No electricity, no mechanical ventilation, no running water. It sounds impossible until you examine the text closely. First, how many animals had to enter the ark? Genesis does not refer to every species alive today, but to each kind or basic family.

[37:48] Researchers who have done the math estimate that only a few thousand animals would have been needed to represent every kind of land animal. And in fact, the average land animal is about the size of a small sheep. They didn't need adult elephants. Young ones would have been enough. Based on those figures, the animals would have occupied less than half the available space. The rest would have held foder, grain, water, and other provisions. Second, the air. Genesis 6 contains an instruction that almost every translation reduces to a window.

[38:20] You shall make a window for the ark and finish it to a cubit above and set the door of the ark in its side. You shall make it with lower, second, and third decks. But the Hebrew word is toar and Hebrew already has another word for window. The very word used later when Noah releases the raven. Tohar means something else. Its root evokes the radiance of midday, the light. Many scholars believe that soar was a continuous opening running the entire length of the vessel just below the roof. Not a tiny window, but a passive ventilation system stretching more than 500 ft. And physics did the rest.

[38:57] Thousands of animals produce heat and gases, ammonia, methane, and carbon dioxide. Without fresh air, death would come within days. But hot air rises and escapes through the upper opening. And that outflow draws fresh air in through the lower openings. Engineers call it the chimney effect. No motors, no moving parts. The vessel breathed on its own. Third, waste. The problem no one wants to talk about. Tons of manure every week for 371 days. Concentrated ammonia kills and accumulated methane explodes. [music] The most plausible solutions are the same ones used in barns throughout history.

[39:41] Gently sloped floors draining into central channels. Manual removal and the air flow from the Soha carrying gases outside before they could reach lethal levels. And fourth, food. God commanded Noah, take with you [music] every kind of food that is eaten. A year's worth of provisions organized by type. Pressed hay, grain, dried fruit, roots, water stored in sealed jars. No detail was unnecessary. No detail was overlooked. [music] But of all the elements of the ark, none carried more symbolism than the door.

[40:24] God had commanded Noah, "You shall [music] set the door of the ark in its side." A single opening in a vessel built to withstand the end of a world. Everything that would survive had to enter through it. And once that door closed, there would be no other way in. When the appointed time came, so did the final warning. God told Noah to enter the ark with his entire family. Time had run out. 7 days remained. Then something extraordinary happened. The animals began to arrive. From the farthest reaches of the earth, a long procession of animals made its way toward the ark.

[40:57] Elephants, lions, deer, and birds of [music] every color and size converged on a single point as if guided by an invisible force. The text simply says that they came to Noah, predator, walking alongside prey without violence, [music] each creature taking its place. They entered with Noah two by two, male and female, one after another. The creatures filed in and disappeared inside that enormous wooden structure. Then the family entered. Noah, his wife, his sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth, and his sons wives, eight people in all, eight out of an entire civilization.

## Part 5 · 41:38

[41:38] The last of the food was stored away. The last animals crossed the threshold. Then came one of the most unsettling moments in the entire story. The door closed. But Genesis does not say that Noah closed it. It says that God shut him inside and the Lord shut him in. The man had spent decades building, cutting, hauling, assembling, sealing [music] with pitch. Yet the one thing he did not do was the final one. Seal the door. What was beyond human strength, God did. Now there was no turning back. 7 days later, the flood began. A sound far more violent than any storm.

[42:17] All the fountains of the great deep burst open and the floodgates of the heavens were opened. Notice the order of that sentence. First the deep. Before a single drop fell, the earth burst open from below. Pressurized underground waters, violent tremors and fractures opening deep within the ground. Water surged up from below and poured down from above. The entire earth was trapped between the two. Noah's family felt the ark tremble before they ever saw the rain. Noah was 600 years old. Genesis even records the exact day, the 17th day of the second month.

[42:56] That date marked the moment when the world Noah knew began to disappear. It rained for one day, then another, then 10, 20, and it did not stop. 40 days and 40 nights of continuous rain. The water began to cover everything. The lowlands disappeared first, then the fields, the roads, the trees, the high ground. The water kept rising until the moment Noah had worked toward for years finally came. The ark lifted off the ground. That massive structure which had stood motionless on dry land for so long began to float. There was no ground beneath it anymore, only water.

[43:37] The ark was not sailing toward any destination. All they could do was try to survive. Their very existence depended on those timbers sealed with pitch. And one detail completely changes the scale of the story. The flood did not end after 40 days of rain. The waters continued to cover the earth for 150 days. 5 months. 5 months surrounded by water. No dry land. No idea when they would be able to leave the ark, not even knowing what they would find outside when it was all over. Then Genesis introduces one of the most important lines in the entire story. God remembered Noah.

[44:17] It was not that God had forgotten him. In Hebrew, to remember means to act on someone's behalf. The silence was never abandonment. It was the prelude to what came next. A wind began to blow across the earth. The springs of the deep closed. The floodgates of heaven stopped pouring down water, and little by little, almost imperceptibly at first, the water [music] began to recede. Then on the 17th day of the seventh month, something happened that must have been felt throughout the entire structure. The ark came to a stop. After months of drifting on the waters, it had touched land.

[44:54] Genesis says it came to rest on the mountains of Ararat, the very place where the outline stands today. But they still could not leave. There was still water outside, a vast amount of water. Touching land did not mean the world was habitable. Noah and his family had survived the flood, but they remained trapped inside the vessel. More weeks passed. The water continued to recede slowly. Then, in the 10th month, something finally appeared that they had not seen for a very long time, the mountaintops. Noah waited another 40 days. Then he opened the arks window.

[45:36] After months confined among wood, animals, and darkness, [music] he needed to know what remained of the outside world. First he released a raven. [music] The bird flew back and forth as the waters continued to recede. Then he released a dove. The dove flew off, searching for a place to land, but it found none. There was still too much water, so it returned to the ark. Noah reached out his hand, took the dove, [music] and brought it back inside. He waited 7 days. Then he released it again. Hours passed [music] and at dusk the dove reappeared but this time it carried something in its beak.

[46:11] A fresh olive leaf. It was small, just a single leaf. But after so many months surrounded by nothing but water, [music] that leaf meant there was land somewhere. There were trees. Branches were growing again. There was life. Noah waited another 7 days and sent the dove out again. And this time it did not [music] return. The message was clear. The outside world was changing, but Noah still did not leave. He waited for a sign from God. Finally, he removed part of the covering and looked outside. The surface of the earth was beginning to dry.

[46:50] [music] The water that had covered everything for months was disappearing. Noah was already 600 years old when he received the command he had been waiting for. Ever since that door closed, after more than a full year inside the ark, God commanded him, "Come out of the ark." And suddenly the entrance opened. Noah stepped out. Then his wife, his three sons, and their wives, and behind them, the animals that had survived the flood began to leave the ark. And so they set foot on solid ground once again. They had entered one world and emerged into another.

[47:26] The first thing Noah did was not build a house. Nor did he search for food or explore the land. Noah built an altar. He took clean animals and offered sacrifices to God. It was the first act of that new world. Then God established a covenant with Noah, his descendants, and every living creature that had come out of the ark. As long as the earth endured seed time and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, day and night, would never cease. And God once again gave a command that echoed the [music] very beginning of humanity. Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth.

[48:04] Then the sign appeared, a rainbow among the clouds. The rainbow became the symbol of the covenant. Never again would the waters become a flood that destroyed all life on earth in that way. But perhaps the most powerful image in Noah's story had appeared long before the rainbow. What skeptics dismissed as impossible for centuries, science now recognizes as a masterpiece, one of humanity's greatest achievements. For generations, many viewed the story of Noah as impossible.

[48:40] But the more its dimensions, structure, and purpose are studied, the harder it becomes to argue that it came from Noah's imagination. The design came from God. He provided the measurements. He gave the instructions. He announced the disaster before it came. and he chose a righteous man of integrity to endure when everything else disappeared. And perhaps that is the most powerful detail. Noah built according to a word from God. He built because he believed in God. While everyone else trusted only what they could see, Noah spent years building something based solely on what God had said.

[49:09] And when the flood came, everything that had seemed absurd became the only safe place on earth. But the ark was never merely a story of survival. It was a picture of something far greater. There was a refuge. There was only one door. And when judgment began, salvation was inside. That pattern runs throughout the entire Bible. Before judgment, God offers refuge. Before condemnation, he opens a way. Before mankind can save itself, God has already prepared a way out. And centuries later, that principle would find its ultimate fulfillment.

[49:51] No longer through a gigantic wooden structure, but through a person, Jesus Christ. Centuries later, Jesus Christ would speak words that make the parallel impossible to ignore. I am the door. I am the way, the truth, and the life. The ark saved Noah from the waters. Christ came to save mankind from something far greater. The plan that began long before the flood continued through generations, prophets, kings, and covenants until it culminated at the cross. Because in the end, the story of the ark isn't just about how eight people survived. It's about how God saves.

[50:29] One refuge, one door, one way, and that way is Jesus Christ.
